## Observed Facts

- **KERNEL is the Component with the most severe entries.** It has 4,324,651 Log Entries in total, and 626,450 of them are at level FATAL. That is the largest FATAL count of any Component [E3]. Across the dataset, KERNEL accounts for 4,324,651 of 4,747,963 Log Entries [E1].
- **APP is the second Component to watch.** It has 228,536 Log Entries, all at level FATAL [E4]. Its per-Log-Entry FATAL share is higher than KERNEL's, but its volume is much smaller.
- **Other Components are much smaller.** DISCOVERY has 97,172 Log Entries and MMCS has 88,930 [E1]. Neither is broken out by level here.
- **FATAL is the largest severity level overall:** 855,195 Log Entries, of which KERNEL and APP account for 626,450 and 228,536 [E2][E3][E4].

Data Scope for all counts: BGL dataset, full time range, no filters.

## Hypotheses

- KERNEL is the biggest risk by measured volume of FATAL entries. Its FATAL count (626,450) is about 2.7 times APP's (228,536) and about 73% of all FATAL entries in the dataset [E2][E3][E4].
- APP is a close second. Every APP entry is FATAL, so it may be a concentrated fault source even though its volume is smaller.

## Unknowns

- Whether FATAL in BGL marks a real system failure or is a routine label in this log format. The logs don't show this.
- Whether these entries had any effect on service, users, or revenue. The logs can't establish downtime, customer impact, or financial loss.
- How the FATAL entries are distributed over time. I have not checked whether they are a recent spike or steady. A trend query would answer this.
- Whether the same underlying fault produces many entries. Log Entries are not incidents, so these counts overstate the number of distinct problems.

## Next Step

Run a trend on KERNEL FATAL entries (by day) to see whether the 626,450 are growing, recurring, or a one-off spike. If that is not already known, also check whether APP's FATAL entries follow the same pattern.
